newsitem.title: FRANCE: Chernomyrdin meets Chirac, tsarist debt on agenda.
newsitem.headline: Chernomyrdin meets Chirac, tsarist debt on agenda.

text.p: Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin met French President Jacques Chirac on Tuesday after pledging to resolve a dispute with Paris over its tsarist debt that has blocked trade in a new Russian bond in France.

The Russian premier, in Paris for a two-day visit, said before leaving Moscow that Russia would pay the debt run up by its pre-1917 tsarist government and repudiated by the Soviet Union after the communist revolution.
The dispute marred Russia's return to international capital markets last week with an oversubscribed $1.0 billion Eurobond, its first debt offering since the 1917 revolution.

France banned trading in the bonds pending settlement of the compensation issue. The descendants of the original French buyers are claiming some 140-160 billion francs ($27 billion to $31 billion), mostly in unpaid interest.

The dispute is also seen as an obstacle to Russia joining the powerful Paris Club of government creditors, which France chairs, a move that would allow it to negotiate the return of Soviet-era debts owed to Moscow, mainly by developing countries.

Asked as he prepared to leave for Paris on Monday whether Russia would pay the debts, Chernomyrdin told reporters: "I think today we will resolve this question. We will because we are Russia. We will pay all our debts."
Speculation about his intentions prompted the Paris bourse to suspend trade in the pre-revolutionary bonds.
Russian Deputy Finance Minister Mikhail Kasyanov, responsible for foreign debt, accompanied Chernomyrdin to France to discuss the tsarist debt issue.
But officials in Moscow and Paris doubted there would be a deal on Tuesday, saying negotiations were complex.

An estimated 1.2 million French investors bought Russian bonds issued up to 1917 to fund projects like the Trans-Siberian railway. The bond holders' association estimates that 400,000 people hold them today.
It said Moscow has settled smaller debt disputes with holders of pre-tsarist bonds in Britain, the United States, Canada and Switzerland.
The Soviet refusal to meet the obligations of its tsarist predecessor left savers holding virtually worthless, if attractively printed, paper.
It was unclear how much Moscow would be prepared to pay, but Chernomyrdin said the timing of repayment would be discussed.
Moscow has argued that any liability for Tsarist-era debt must be offset against the seizure in the West of Russian assets, which were used to help fight the Communists.
Chernomyrdin has been virtually running Russia while President Boris Yeltsin convalesces from heart bypass surgery, which was performed on November 5.

After talks with the conservative Chirac, Chernomyrdin was to join French Prime Minister Alain Juppe at a meeting of a bilateral commission on Franco-Russian economic ties and hold a joint news conference with Juppe at 1630 GMT.

Later on Tuesday, Chernomyrdin was to hold private talks with Juppe followed by a dinner. On Wednesday he was scheduled to meet National Assembly speaker Philippe Seguin and French business leaders before leaving for Poland on Thursday.
Talks were to centre on economic ties and international matters including Moscow's relations with NATO and its opposition to eastern expansion of the Atlantic alliance.
